before.label: Economic history
before.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000).

before.label: New social history
before.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
before.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996).

before.scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

after.scope_note: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963) and the 1971 lectures distinguish successive historical perspectives. James later sought closer study of rank-and-file leaders and praised Du Bois’s attention to political imagination. His recollections identify Trotsky, Lenin and Marx among resources, alongside Caribbean projects. Beyond a Boundary (1963) examines social divisions through clubs and treats cricket as an art. These connections do not make him a disciple of postwar British social history.

before.label: Eric Williams
before.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.

after.label: Eric Williams
after.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. after.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
after.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.
